# Seonangshin and the industries that were always telling its story

The myths did not retire. They moved offices. This is the file on where **Seonangshin** works now.

Seonangshin has no epic cycle; her mythology is the living archive of Korean village religion — boundary shrines, communal rites, and origin legends recorded in classical miscellanies such as the Samguk Yusa and the nineteenth-century Dongguk Sesigi, then catalogued by twentieth-century folklore surveys. The narratives vary by region and by shamanic lineage, and the record says so.

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) — which maps every flagship temple to the industries its archetype demonstrably resonates with, each match argued and open to challenge — seats this temple in **3 industries**. This file reads those seats the way they were earned: through the myths.

## The Myth at Work

**The Shrine at the Village Gate.** Every traditional Korean village kept a seonangdang, a small open shrine set where the settlement's paths met the fields — the precise point where cultivated space gave way to mountain and wild.  The nineteenth-century miscellany Dongguk Sesigi (1849) describes the offerings made there: rice wine poured out, lengths of cloth hung, the season's first fruits presented, and prayers spoken to keep epidemic and disaster outside the settlement. — that is not just a story. It is a business model, four thousand years early.

**Guardian of the Threshold.** Korean village religion builds its boundary in visible grammar: the geumjul, a twisted straw rope hung with paper strips and dried gourds, declares sacred space; the jangseung, grinning wooden posts carved in the likeness of generals, stand sentinel at the paths; the sotdae, tall poles topped with carved birds, lift the village's wishes skyward.  Seonangshin was imagined moving among these markers as a patrolling official or armed warrior, inspecting the fence between the human world and the wilderness. — that is not just a story. It is a business model, four thousand years early.

## The Long Employment

Seonangshin remains visible in the Korean cultural landscape: guardian trees, stone cairns, jangseung posts, and restored seonangdang shrines stand in heritage villages such as Hahoe and Yangdong, inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2010, and on Jeju the island's stone seonangdang cairns are protected as folk heritage.  Urban Korea keeps the learned cousin of the cult alive in seonghwang shrines, and the dongje survives wherever a village still gathers — as rite, as festival, or as tourist calendar. The age changed. The work did not.
